plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a color-coded periodic table of the elements annotated with the most common ionic charges formed by main-group and selected transition-metal elements, illustrating the relationship between an element's position in the table and its tendency to form ions. Group 1 elements (Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+, Fr+, shaded purple) and Group 2 elements (Be2+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+, Ra2+, shaded green) form cations with charges equal to their group number, while nonmetals in Groups 15–17 (shaded pink) form anions such as N3−, O2−, F−, P3−, S2−, Cl−, and their congeners, with negative charges reflecting how many groups they lie to the left of the noble gases. Transition metals in the central d-block (shaded tan) display variable charges — for example Cr3+/Cr6+, Fe2+/Fe3+, Cu+/Cu2+, and Au+/Au3+ — demonstrating that their ionic behavior is not reliably predicted by group position alone. Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, shaded blue) carry no charge label, reflecting their chemical inertness. This figure establishes the periodic trends in ion formation and marks the boundary where the group-number rule reliably predicts ionic charge versus where transition-metal variability and other exceptions require additional consideration.

interactionPlan.concept: An element's group position reliably predicts its common ionic charge for main-group elements (cations equal to the group number, anions equal to the steps left of the noble gases), but transition metals break this rule by forming several variable charges.

interactions.label: Group number
interactions.teaches: Sweeping the groups left to right makes the systematic trend visible: groups 1-2 form cations whose positive charge equals the group number, groups 15-17 form anions whose negative charge equals 18 minus the group number, and the central d-block refuses a single value

Selecting one cell reveals that element's specific ion charge, its electron configuration, and the group-trend rule that explains the charge — showing the charge is just the count of electrons lost or gained to reach a stable (often noble-gas) configuration

interactions.label: Color scheme
interactions.teaches: Comparing element-type coloring with charge-value coloring shows that the charge pattern is not random: it tracks the metal/nonmetal/noble-gas classification, and recoloring by charge magnitude makes the smooth +2 -> 0 -> -3 sweep across a period pop out

demo_steps.title: Cations on the left
demo_steps.narration: With element-type coloring and the slider on group 1, the highlighted column shows every alkali metal as a +1 cation; group 2 is +2. The positive charge simply equals the group number because these metals lose their outer electrons.

demo_steps.title: Anions on the right
demo_steps.narration: Sweep the slider to group 17: the halogens are all -1, group 16 is -2, group 15 is -3. The negative charge equals 18 minus the group number — the electrons needed to complete the noble-gas shell.

demo_steps.title: Transition metals break the rule
demo_steps.narration: Move the slider into the d-block (e.g. group 8) and click iron: it shows Fe2+ AND Fe3+, with no single group-number rule. Click chromium or copper to see the same variability — position alone cannot predict transition-metal charge.

demo_steps.title: Two ways to see the same pattern
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to ion-charge coloring: the table recolors by charge magnitude, turning the metal-to-nonmetal transition into a smooth visual gradient and making the noble-gas column (charge 0) read as the neutral pivot of the whole trend.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: For main-group elements the common ionic charge is read straight off the group number (lose that many electrons, or gain up to the noble-gas configuration), but transition metals form multiple variable charges that no group-position rule can predict.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out a standard 18-column periodic grid with group numbers 1-18 in blue along the top and period numbers 1-7 in purple down the left. Color families exactly as in the source: group 1 purple, group 2 green, d-block tan/cream, groups 15-16 pink, group 17 lavender, group 18 cyan, remaining p-block cells white. Write each element's common ion charge inside its cell, stacking two charges (e.g. Cr3+/Cr6+, Fe2+/Fe3+, Cu+/Cu2+, Au+/Au3+, Hg2 2+/Hg2+) where the element is variable. Leave noble gases and the period-1 hydrogen cell without a charge. Draw a red rectangle around the group-3 cells of periods 6-7 with a curved red arrow pointing to two detached strips below (green lanthanides *, pink actinides **). For the slider, outline or brighten the active column; for click, draw a bold highlight ring on the chosen cell plus a small info card with charge, electron configuration, and the governing rule; for the toggle, swap the per-cell fill from the element-type palette to a charge-magnitude palette (deep warm for high positive, neutral gray for 0, deep cool for high negative).

authoredContext:
Note the usefulness of the periodic table in predicting likely ion formation and charge ( ). Moving from the far left to the right on the periodic table, main-group elements tend to form cations with a charge equal to the group number. That is, group 1 elements form 1+ ions; group 2 elements form 2+ ions, and so on. Moving from the far right to the left on the periodic table, elements often form anions with a negative charge equal to the number of groups moved left from the noble gases. For example, group 17 elements (one group left of the noble gases) form 1− ions; group 16 elements (two groups left) form 2− ions, and so on. This trend can be used as a guide in many cases, but its predictive value decreases when moving toward the center of the periodic table. In fact, transition metals and some other metals often exhibit variable charges that are not predictable by their location in the table. For example, copper can form ions with a 1+ or 2+ charge, and iron can form ions with a 2+ or 3+ charge.

Some elements exhibit a regular pattern of ionic charge when they form ions.

A periodic table showing common ion charges. Group one contains lithium superscript plus, sodium superscript plus, potassium superscript plus, rubidium superscript plus, cesium superscript plus, and francium superscript plus. Group two contains beryllium superscript 2 plus, magnesium superscript 2 plus, calcium superscript 2 plus, strontium superscript 2 plus, barium superscript 2 plus, and radium superscript 2 plus. Group six contains chromium superscript 3 plus and chromium superscript 6 plus. Group seven contains manganese superscript 2 plus. Group eight contains iron superscript 2 plus and iron superscript 3 plus. Group nine contains cobalt superscript 2 plus. Group ten contains nickel superscript 2 plus and platinum superscript 2 plus. Group 11 contains copper superscript plus and copper superscript 2 plus, silver superscript plus, and gold superscript plus and gold superscript 3 plus. Group 12 contains zinc superscript 2 plus, cadmium superscript 2 plus, and mercury superscript 2 plus and mercury subscript 2 superscript 2 plus. Group 13 contains aluminum superscript 3 plus. Group 14 contains carbon superscript 4 minus. Group 15 contains nitrogen superscript 3 minus, phosphorus superscript 3 minus, and arsenic superscript 3 minus. Group 16 contains oxygen superscript 2 minus, sulfur superscript 2 minus, selenium superscript 2 minus, and tellurium superscript 2 minus. Group 17 contains fluorine superscript minus, chlorine superscript minus, bromine superscript minus, iodine superscript minus, and astatine superscript minus. Group 18 contains helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon, with no charges indicated.

The ions that we have discussed so far are called monatomic ions , that is, they are ions formed from only one atom. We also find many polyatomic ions . These ions, which act as discrete units, are electrically charged molecules (a group of bonded atoms with an overall charge). Some of the more important polyatomic ions are listed in . Oxyanions are polyatomic ions that contain one or more oxygen atoms. At this point in your study of chemistry, you should memorize the names, formulas, and charges of the most common polyatomic ions. Because you will use them repeatedly, they will soon become familiar.

discrepancies: The centered title 'Periodic Table of the Elements' overlaps the blue group-number row and the 'Group' axis label at the top, producing a visible text collision not present in the source.

Ion-charge text (Li⁺, Be²⁺, Cr³⁺/Cr⁶⁺, etc.) and the group/period numbers render too small to read comfortably at inline size because the 980-wide viewbox is squeezed into the left half beside the docked UI panel.
The 'Group' axis label is centered over the middle of the table (above ~group 5) instead of sitting at the top-left above group 1 as in the source.
The 'Color by ion charge' mode recolors cells gold/red/blue with no on-figure legend, so the new color mapping is unexplained visually.
Source leaves the period-7 d-block and several p-block cells blank/white; the generated version matches this but the tiny font makes blank-vs-filled cells harder to distinguish than in the source.
evaluation.notes: The 18x7 grid, element-type color scheme, ion-charge annotations, red group-3 box, curved arrow, and two-row f-block all faithfully reproduce the source, and the group-sweep slider, charge-coloring toggle, four demo steps, and click-for-config info card are functional and on-concept; the main weaknesses are a title/group-number collision, an off-position 'Group' label, sub-legible cell text at inline size, and the absence of a legend for the charge-color mode.
action_items: Increase the top margin (topM) and/or lower the title's y so 'Periodic Table of the Elements' no longer collides with the blue group-number row and the 'Group' label.
Enlarge cell font sizes (or reduce the viewbox width / give the SVG more horizontal space) so ion-charge superscripts and group/period numbers are comfortably readable at inline render size.
Move the 'Group' axis label to the top-left directly above group 1 to match the source layout.
When 'Color by ion charge' is enabled, draw a small color legend (e.g. +1/+2/+3, -1/-2/-3, variable) so the recoloring is self-explanatory.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are solid (scores mostly 4), and all action items are concrete implementation fixes — title collision, font sizing, label repositioning, and adding a charge-color legend — requiring no plan changes.

Replace the thin red connector with a thick gray-filled curved arrow and a bold red-outlined arrowhead to match the source's f-block pointer.
Increase cell dimensions or in-cell font size (and the two-line charge layout) so superscript charges like Cr3+/Cr6+ and Hg2 2+/Hg2+ are comfortably legible at inline size.
